citations.evidenceText:
Mapping: Four Ways to Store a Map
•  Occupancy grid
    – World split into cells; each holds Probability that it is occupied by an obstacle. Simple,
       easy to plan.
    –  Typical use: indoor cleaning robot
•   Feature map
    – Only landmarks: corners, poles, markers. Very compact, needs good perception.
    –  Typical use: warehouse AGV
•   Topological map
    – Nodes and edges — 'room A connects to corridor B'. Tiny, no metric detail.
    –  typical use: building-scale routing
•   Point cloud/mesh
    –  Millions of 3D points from LiDAR or RGB-D. Rich, heavy to store.
    –  typical use: inspection & 3-D scanning
•  Many real systems keep two at once — a point cloud for perception
   and a coarse grid for planning.

optionExplanations.o3: Representations preserve task-relevant environmental information at different detail and storage levels; the source explicitly allows two maps at once.
optionExplanations.o4: Sparse landmarks do not encode every surface point without an additional surface model.

Pose Graph SLAM

•  The ever-growing state vector and covariance matrix makes it difficult to map
   large-scale areas like city blocks/complex buildings.

   consistent solution.
•  Pose-Graph SLAM provides an alternative formulation of

    – A Region of Interest (ROI) is defined directly in front of the
       robot (red triangle), where immediate foreground is assumed to be obstacle-free.
    – The color and texture features within this region are sampled as a reference model
        of a safe traversable surface for subsequent obstacle detection.
4.  Mask Generation and Pixel Classification
    – Each pixel in far-view region is compared with ROI reference
        using predefined color tolerance thresholds (e.g., ±15 intensity
         levels) and classified as either traversable or non-traversable.
    – The classification results are stored in a binary mask, which is
       subsequently refined using morphological erosion to remove
        isolated noise and strengthen the boundaries of the detected
        safe traversable area.

concepts.title: Purpose of a map
concepts.description: A map stores task-relevant environmental information. Rich point clouds or meshes support inspection but are storage-heavy; a coarse occupancy grid can support planning, while sparse feature maps retain selected landmarks compactly.

concepts.title: Occupancy-grid meaning
concepts.description: An occupancy grid assigns obstacle-occupancy information to spatial cells.

concepts.title: Choosing a map representation
concepts.description: A feature map stores a compact set of detectable landmarks and their positions.

concepts.title: Topological versus geometric detail
concepts.description: Nodes and edges express connectivity; a bare graph need not provide detailed metric geometry.

concepts.title: Hybrid map roles
concepts.description: The representations can serve different tasks instead of requiring one representation to do everything.

concepts.title: State under ideal localization
concepts.description: The map-only state contains two coordinates per landmark and excludes the known robot pose.

concepts.title: Initial map state
concepts.description: The estimator begins with an empty landmark map and adds two values for each newly observed landmark.

concepts.title: Static-landmark prediction
concepts.description: The static identity transition with zero process noise leaves the existing landmark mean and covariance unchanged.

concepts.title: Converting a range-bearing observation
concepts.description: The world bearing is 90°−90°=0°, so the observation adds (4,0) to (2,3).

concepts.title: Dimensionally consistent map augmentation
concepts.description: The derivative of the copied2M-coordinate old map is I_2M, and the new point depends on the independent measurement through Gz. Thus J=diag(I_2M,Gz) and Σ′=diag(Σ,GzWGzᵀ). This is a known-pose, independent-new-measurement example, not a claim that arbitrary SLAM maps have zero correlations.

concepts.title: Known pose versus a zero derivative
concepts.description: Knowing a variable exactly removes its uncertainty contribution, not the mathematical dependence of the inverse model on that variable.
concepts.subtopic: Known pose versus a zero derivative

concepts.title: Inverse-observation uncertainty directions
concepts.description: At zero world bearing, range changes world x by one per meter and bearing changes world y by r per radian.

concepts.title: Covariance of a new landmark
concepts.description: Gz=diag(1,4), so Gz W Gzᵀ scales the bearing variance by 4², giving 0.0064 m².

concepts.title: Correct bearing quadrant
concepts.description: atan2(dy,dx) uses both coordinate signs and returns 135° for the second quadrant.

concepts.title: Wrapping an angular innovation
concepts.description: Raw subtraction gives −358°, which is equivalent to +2° after adding 360°.

concepts.title: Landmark observation derivative
concepts.description: The range is 5; its derivatives are dx/r and dy/r, while bearing derivatives are −dy/r² and dx/r².

concepts.title: Observed-landmark block in H
concepts.description: The local observation model uses the selected landmark position, so other landmark blocks have zero direct observation derivatives.

concepts.title: Measurement innovation meaning
concepts.description: The innovation is a residual in measurement space, z−h(predicted state), with angular residuals handled consistently.

concepts.title: True simulation map versus estimator input
concepts.description: The sensor’s ground-truth map generates observations; omitting the EKF map input selects map estimation rather than known-map localization.
concepts.subtopic: True simulation map versus estimator input

concepts.title: Covariance from standard deviations
concepts.description: The range standard deviation 0.1 m is squared to obtain variance 0.01 m².

concepts.title: Finite sensor visibility
concepts.description: Three meters is within 4 m and 60° lies in the frontal ±90° interval.

concepts.title: Interpreting the simulated estimated map
concepts.description: Limited range, field of view and the traveled path can leave true landmarks unobserved.

concepts.title: Localization, mapping and SLAM
concepts.description: Simultaneous localization and mapping jointly estimates pose and map.

concepts.title: Why localization and mapping are coupled
concepts.description: The two unknowns inform each other, motivating joint or coupled estimation.
concepts.subtopic: Why localization and mapping are coupled

concepts.title: Planar SLAM state size
concepts.description: It has three robot-pose components plus sixteen landmark coordinates: 3+2×8=19.

concepts.title: Robot-map covariance shape
concepts.description: Rows correspond to the three pose variables and columns to the 2M map coordinates.

concepts.description: Differentiate the cosine and sine position terms with respect to heading.

concepts.title: Converting initial uncertainties
concepts.description: Square each standard deviation and use zero cross-covariance under the stated independence.

concepts.title: Predicting the 1D SLAM state
concepts.description: Only the robot mean advances, and independent robot motion variance adds to its prior variance.

concepts.title: One-dimensional measurement model
concepts.description: Increasing robot position decreases the signed separation; increasing landmark position increases it.

concepts.title: Innovation variance in the 1D update
concepts.description: The two state variances contribute 0.5+1, and measurement variance adds 0.25, giving 1.75.

concepts.description: P Hᵀ=(−0.5,1)ᵀ; division by 1.75 gives (−2/7,4/7)ᵀ.

concepts.title: What map alignment establishes
concepts.description: Rigid alignment can reconcile translation and rotation between frames; it does not generally repair local geometric distortions or prove absolute observability.

concepts.title: EKF information from earlier observations
concepts.description: A joint state of dimension n=3+2M uses n scalar state entries and n² entries if its full covariance is stored. The covariance summarizes accumulated information, including correlations; a pose graph instead explicitly represents constraints among multiple poses. Quadratic storage is not a universal runtime claim.

concepts.title: Edges in a pose-landmark graph
concepts.description: Odometry relates successive robot poses; observations relate robot poses to environmental landmarks.

concepts.title: Checking a planar rotation matrix

concepts.title: Relative pose from world poses

concepts.description: The displayed sequence illustrates iterative refinement of pose estimates for accumulated constraints.

concepts.description: The front end interprets sensing and motion into constraints, while the back end solves the resulting estimation problem.

concepts.description: Local relationships make many direct Jacobian blocks zero, allowing sparse numerical methods.

concepts.title: Qualifying the resource argument
concepts.description: The lecture presents pseudo-random navigation as inexpensive but inefficient for goal-directed tasks. Lightweight perception can serve some tasks, while SLAM’s actual requirements depend on sensors, algorithms, hardware and the required behavior.

concepts.title: Structure from Motion limitation
concepts.description: Recovering structure from moving-camera images depends on informative visual observations and correspondences.

concepts.title: The immediate-floor assumption
concepts.description: The red triangle is a reference-region annotation, not the unsafe class label. The reference is assumed clear and representative. Rays begin at the image bottom-center and stop at the first red non-floor pixel after a green floor prefix; this does not certify physical safety or calibrate the schematic row spacing.

concepts.title: Visual attributes used by Floor Finder
concepts.description: The described method combines color, brightness and texture-related attributes rather than relying on one color value.

concepts.title: Texture versus color
concepts.description: The slide lists both color and texture attributes, so the distinction is from color-only matching, not a prohibition on color.

concepts.title: A contaminated reference patch
concepts.description: The reference assumes floor; contaminating it can corrupt the appearance model used for later classification.

concepts.title: Pixel-count reduction
concepts.description: Both dimensions are halved, so the pixel count is reduced by 2×2=4.

concepts.title: Downsampling trade-off
concepts.description: Downsampling reduces the number of samples, which can lower cost while losing fine spatial detail.

concepts.title: Preserving image geometry when resizing
concepts.description: 1900/1200 differs from 320/240; an unqualified resize can scale horizontal and vertical coordinates differently.

concepts.title: Purpose and limitation of Gaussian smoothing
concepts.description: Smoothing reduces rapid image variation but can also blur boundaries and small objects.
concepts.subtopic: Purpose and limitation of Gaussian smoothing

concepts.title: Support of repeated smoothing
concepts.description: Each additional five-tap convolution expands the support by four: 1+3×(5−1)=13.

concepts.title: Applying a stated pixel tolerance
concepts.description: The inclusive interval is [85,115], so 115 is accepted.

concepts.title: Three-by-three erosion rule
concepts.description: Binary erosion with a full 3×3 structuring element requires every covered pixel to be foreground.

concepts.title: Eroding a rectangular floor patch
concepts.description: One border layer is removed from every side, leaving (7−2)×(5−2)=5×3=15.

concepts.title: What floor-mask erosion can remove
concepts.description: An isolated foreground pixel lacks the required all-floor neighborhood and disappears.

concepts.title: Stopping at the first non-floor pixel
concepts.description: The first non-floor sample ends the connected floor segment; later floor-like samples are ignored along that ray.

concepts.title: Pixel counts versus metric distance
concepts.description: Image coordinates alone are not metric distances; camera geometry supplies the required relationship.

concepts.description: The numerator is 500×0.4=200 pixel-meters and the denominator is 50 pixels, giving 4 m.

concepts.description: For rows below the horizon, z=200/(v−200); the smallest positive denominator gives the farthest depth.

concepts.description: The numerator and pixel offset both halve, so their ratio remains 4 m.

concepts.title: Distance sensitivity near the horizon
concepts.description: The denominator of the derivative shrinks, making depth estimates increasingly sensitive near the horizon.

concepts.title: Asynchronous graph-building and optimization
concepts.description: The front end builds measurement relationships while periodic back-end optimization updates a consistent graph estimate; timing and feedback are separate from a simple role label.

concepts.title: Joint versus map-only observation Jacobian
concepts.description: Joint SLAM includes pose and observed-landmark sensitivity; a map-only Jacobian would omit the uncertain-pose block. Unobserved landmarks have zero direct columns even though covariance can propagate their update.
